title: not fate, not payback
hook: a robber asks if his family will share his deeds; what karma really means
tomorrow: what your grandmother was actually doing

segments.voice: Yesterday: one truth, many names, and the one that's yours. Six words so far: Ganesha, om, Gayatri, namaste, arti, ishta devata. Today, the seventh.
screen: `GANESHA · OM · GAYATRI · NAMASTE · ARTI · ISHTA DEVATA`

segments.voice: Karma. Someone says it when the car that cut them off gets stuck at the next light. Used like that, it means payback: the universe keeping score. The older meaning turns the whole thing around, and a well-loved story shows how. Long before he was a poet, the story goes, Valmiki was a robber on a forest road. One day he stopped a wandering sage, who asked him a question. You rob to feed your family. Will they share what your deeds bring you? The robber went home and asked. One by one, they said no. What you do is yours. He came back shaken, sat down to meditate, and sat so long that an anthill grew over him. The story says that's where his name comes from: valmika, an anthill. The robber became the poet of the Ramayana.
screen: `KARMA.` → `A ROBBER ON A FOREST ROAD.` → `WHAT YOU DO IS YOURS.` → `FROM ROBBER TO POET.`

segments.voice: Karma is the Sanskrit word for action. A deed. Something done. Krishna teaches that no one can stay without acting, even for a moment: breathing, speaking, choosing, all of it is action. So karma isn't something that happens to you. It's what you do. And what does action do back? One of the oldest Hindu texts says it like a proverb: as a person acts, so that person becomes. Not: so the person is punished. Becomes. Patience, practiced, makes a patient person. Sharpness, practiced, makes a sharp one. That's what the robber learned: no one could carry his deeds for him, and no one could stop him from changing them. The payback version keeps your eyes on other people. The older version turns you around: what am I becoming with my next word? Hindu teachers also speak of karma across lifetimes; that's a bigger conversation for later. For today: as you act, so you become.
screen: `KARMA — ACTION, A DEED` · `AS ONE ACTS, SO ONE BECOMES` · `NO ONE CARRIES YOUR DEEDS` · `WHAT AM I BECOMING?`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Bring to mind one small thing you did this week: a kind word, a sharp one, a promise kept or skipped. Don't grade it. Just ask what it's growing. Then pick one small action you'd be glad to see grow.
Karma. Action, and what action makes of the one who does it. Not payback. Seventh word: a week's worth.
Your line: what you do, you become. That's week one: seven words, and what's inside each. Tomorrow, what your grandmother was actually doing.

story.title: the robber's question
story.text: A well-loved telling says the poet Valmiki started out as a robber. One day he tried to rob a wandering sage, who asked him a question: would his family share the weight of what he did? He went home and asked. They said no. What he did was his. Shaken, he changed, and became the poet who would compose the Ramayana.
story.source: a traditional telling of Valmiki's life (later than the Ramayana itself)
